From Geometry to Quantum Mechanics
#

Part 26 of the Learning Quantum Physics series.

item.title: Operators in Quantum Mechanics
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
Operators in Quantum Mechanics
#

Part 27 of the Learning Quantum Physics series.

An operator takes the column of a state and returns a new column. On one qubit the column has two entries, so the operator is a 2 by 2 matrix. Write the matrix on the left. Write the column on the right. Multiply.

From Geometry to Quantum Mechanics uses these names side by side with arrows in a plane. This article defines each operator, writes its matrix, and says what the matrix does.

item.title: How Many Numbers Does a Qubit Need?
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
How Many Numbers Does a Qubit Need?
#

You already know how to place a point. On a plane you need two numbers. In a room you need three. This article uses that skill for a qubit.

A qubit is the smallest piece of quantum information. One pure qubit is a point on a sphere. The sphere is the surface of an ordinary ball, so the point has coordinates \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\). Those coordinates obey \(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 1\), so two of the three coordinates are free.

The path there starts with an arrow.

item.title: Building a 20-Qubit Quantum System Using Photons
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
Building a 20-Qubit Quantum System Using Photons
#

Part 13 of the Learning Quantum Physics series.

Quantum computing often becomes difficult to understand because we start directly with symbols such as:

|0>, |1>, superposition, entanglement, Hilbert space, and quantum gates.

A simpler approach is to start with the physical system — the actual hardware — and only then attach the math.

Let us assume that we want to build a 20-qubit quantum system using photons.

The central idea is:

One photon can be used as one qubit if we choose one two-state property of that photon to represent |0> and |1>.

For this article, we will use the polarization of a photon.

If you write software
#

If you already think in bits, registers, and logic gates, here is the mapping this article uses:

Classical computing Photonic qubits (this article)
One bit: 0 or 1 One qubit: two basis states labeled |0> and |1>
20-bit register: one of 2^20 bit strings 20-qubit register: one joint state in a 2^20-dimensional vector space
AND / OR / NOT gates Unitary transforms implemented with wave plates, beam splitters, and phase shifters
Read register → get 20 bits Measure 20 qubits → get one 20-bit outcome per experimental run

The goal is not to memorize optics. It is to see where the symbols in a quantum circuit come from physically — so notation like |0>, |+>, tensor products, and entanglement map to hardware you could, in principle, build in a lab.

Throughout, |0> and |1> are Dirac ket labels (basis state names), not ASCII angle brackets around integers.
